_comment: Navigation sweep profile for Mega Man (1987) (Capcom) - ADR-0239, PRD
Part A slice F14.17. Read by scripts/record_navigation_sweep.py.
RUNG 1, NOT RUNG 2. ADR-0239 s1 says to use the first rung that reaches
the place, and for Mega Man that is rung 1: the game's own STAGE SELECT
screen, reached and driven by input alone. navigation.kind is 'input', so
no cheat rides with any session and every session is an ADR-0184 s2
'clean' pass that all four of ADR-0183's surfaces may read. Rung 2 was
not needed and is not used, even though this game does publish the byte a
selector would pin (below) - the ladder stops at the first rung that
reaches the place, and rung 1 reaches all six robot masters.
THE SELECTOR, AND WHAT IT IS CALLED. From power-on: the title screen
('PRESS START'), Start, and the game is on the screen it labels 'SELECT
STAGE / PRESS START'. Six portraits are drawn in a 3x2 grid with their
names under them - CUTMAN and GUTSMAN on the top row, ELECMAN and ICEMAN
on the middle one, FIREMAN and BOMBMAN on the bottom - and one of them
carries a blinking highlight. The Mega Man instruction booklet (Capcom
USA, 1987; archive.org item 'mega-man-nes-manual', file
'Mega-Man-Game-Manual_djvu.txt') describes it in its own words: 'Six of
MEGA MAN['s] ... enemies will be displayed on the TV/monitor screen.
Player selects the character he chooses to challenge by pressing the
control pad's tip ... Re-press START Button. To begin encounter with the
enemy character selected by the player.' StrategyWiki's control page
('Mega Man/Walkthrough') names the buttons: 'You can switch between Robot
Masters by pressing [Left/Right]. To select a stage, press [A/Start].'
THE RING, AND WHICH KEY WALKS IT. The six portraits are not a grid the
pad walks freely; they are a ring, and Right walks it clockwise one
portrait at a time. Measured on this ROM on 2026-09-26 by entering the
stage each press count reaches and reading both the screen and the
published stage byte:
Right presses   stage entered   $0031   screen
0               Cut Man         00      teal brick columns, grey building
1               Guts Man        05      brown rock face, mine cart
2               Ice Man         01      ice ground, icicle 'palms'
3               Bomb Man        02      bomb-shaped trees, blue sky
4               Fire Man        03      red brick furnace interior
5               Elec Man        04      green circuit board
6               Cut Man         00      the ring closes
so the ring is CUTMAN -> GUTSMAN -> ICEMAN -> BOMBMAN -> FIREMAN ->
ELECMAN -> CUTMAN. The ring order is not the order the booklet's score
table prints, and it is not the order the stage-select screen's own grid
geometry would suggest, which is why it was measured instead of assumed:
from CUTMAN the portrait below it is ELECMAN and the one to its right is
GUTSMAN, but Right from GUTSMAN reaches ICEMAN, not the middle row's left
column. Six entered stages, six distinct byte values and six distinct
screens agree, so the ring is what the game does.
DOWN IS INERT HERE. The vertical axis of the pad does nothing on this
screen: one, two and three Down presses each leave the session
byte-identical to a session with no press at all - same final state, same
screenshot, $0031 = 00 and the CUTMAN stage entered. Right is therefore
the only cursor key this profile uses, and the Left/Right the booklet and
StrategyWiki both name as the pair is really Right for the six moves this
sweep needs.
THE SCREEN NEEDS A MOMENT BEFORE IT READS THE PAD. A Right starting 60
frames after the Start that opened the screen is ignored, and a second
Start that early does not enter the stage either - both sessions end on
the select they started on - while the same Right 240 frames later moves
the cursor and a Start there enters the stage. Every entry script below
therefore idles 240 frames between the Start that opens the screen and the
first press. The presses themselves
are 40 frames with a 60-frame gap; a 40-frame hold is well inside one
screen of the ring and cannot double-step it (measured: one press, one
portrait).
THE RAM CHECK, AND WHY IT IS NOT THE SELECTOR. ADR-0239 s4 prefers a check
on a byte the place sets over one on the selector's own address, and this
profile has no selector address at all: it pins nothing. $0031 is the
byte, published by Data Crystal ('Mega Man (NES)/RAM map', read through
the Wayback Machine on 2026-09-26 - the live page is behind a JS
challenge) as '0x0031 Stage ID, $00-Cut Man ... $0B(11)-Ending BG'. The
map publishes the address and the two endpoints; the six values in the
table above are measured, and a check is not a cheat, so ADR-0184 s5's
source rule does not reach the numbers (the Ninja Gaiden profile set the
same precedent for its room counter).
Two things about the byte are worth writing down because a reader will
otherwise misread a passing check. First, $0031 is STALE while the screen
is merely displayed: a session that reaches the select and never presses
Start ends with $0031 = 01 (Ice Man) even though the highlight is on
CUTMAN, and this profile never reads it there - every check is read off
the session's own final state, which is inside the stage. Second, it is
not a byte the run carries from the menu: the game writes it when the
selected stage loads, which is exactly what makes it evidence that the
warp happened. The one value whose check cannot distinguish a warp from a
flat refusal is CUTMAN's, because 00 is both its own byte and the value a
run that never took the screen at all would end on - its tiles are what
separate the two, and the sweep reports them beside the check.
NO LIVES PIN, SO ADR-0239 s3's INERT CONTROL DOES NOT APPLY. This profile
carries no cheat of any kind: defaults.cheats and values[].cheats are
both absent, no process in this sweep is launched with a cheat= argument,
and the body is allowed to die. Measured on the sweep's own shape: the
120 s Cutman session ends with $00A6 = 0 - the last life, bit 7 clear, so
not GAME OVER - still inside the Cutman stage, with $0031 = 00 and
$006A = 13 of the 28-point life bar left. Deaths and respawns are
recorded, which is what ADR-0184 s4 asks for.
WHY THERE IS NO 'continue' VALUE. ADR-0239 s1's first rung is the game's
own selector, and this game has exactly one: the stage select. The title
screen offers nothing else (it is 'PRESS START' and no more - Start opens
the select, and A at the title was measured to do nothing at all), and
the only other menu the game has is the game-over screen, which
StrategyWiki's gameplay page describes: 'The game over screen is a blue
screen that shows your score. Two choices are given: continue, or select
a level. If you choose to continue, you will begin at the start of the
level you were just playing.' Neither choice is a distinct place: one
restarts the stage the session is already in and the other is this same
stage select. It is also out of the sweep's reach - the 120 s budget ends
with Mega Man alive on his last life (above), so no session of this sweep
reaches GAME OVER at all.
THE SIX VALUES, AND WHAT IS NOT HERE. The six robot masters are the whole
of what the stage select offers, so there is no rooms[] in this profile
and nothing left over for rung 3. NOT reached, and not reachable from a
selector: Dr. Wily's four-stage fortress. The stage select draws it only
once the six portraits' backgrounds have gone black - the booklet's own
words: 'Every time a key character is defeated by MEGA MAN, the
background of enemy's illustration becomes black. When all of Dr. Wily's
programmed humanoids are eliminated, and all backgrounds appear black, Dr.
Wily appears automatically.' That is a stage-clear transition, which
ADR-0239 s1 puts on rung 3 and a later measurement has to name, exactly
like the transition itself.
CAVEAT THAT APPLIES TO EVERY SESSION. The run never clears the stage it
enters - it does not try to - so the stage-clear transition and every
figure that exists only in it are absent from all six recordings
(ADR-0184's 2026-09-14 amendment). The union metric of ADR-0239 s5 makes
that invisible, so it is stated here as well as in the results log.
_provenanceComment: romSha1 above is the WHOLE-FILE SHA1 of the library dump, which is the
hash iNES consumers and HD packs quote; the artist pack for this ROM
names it in its own <patch> line (below, under the reference note). The
No-Intro payload SHA1 of the same file - the identity ADR-0003 pins and
the one a pack's targets[] would carry - is
scripts/mep_build.py's _no_intro_sha1. The ROM is the user's own dump and
is never copied into the repository.
The dump is 131 088 bytes: an 8-bank PRG (128 KB) and ZERO CHR banks, so
this is a UxROM (iNES mapper 2) board with CHR RAM. Two consequences
follow for ADR-0239 s5, and both are in runs/f1417/megaman/RESULT.md:
s5.2's ROM CHR denominator does not exist for this game, and a PRG patch
can reach the tile data, because the graphics are unpacked out of PRG
into CHR RAM at run time (ADR-0184 s1's hazard 1, which is why the
artist pack on disk is refused below).
_referenceComment: ADR-0239 s5.3's reference row is REFUSED for this game, not absent
because a pack is missing. There is exactly one artist pack for this ROM
on this machine, and it is keyed to a patched ROM:
<path>/HdPacks/Mega Man (1987) (Capcom)/hires.txt
<patch>Megaman - Super.ips,2F88381557339A14C20428455F6991C1EB902C99
<patch>Megaman - Super.ips,51A9FE7B5CB82833FC416E0F29B965495D9CE49A
The first <patch> hash is this dump's own whole-file SHA1, so the patch
applies here, and the pack's own README says the patch is not optional:
'Make sure when the game starts that there is text at the bottom stating
"[Patch] Applying Patch: Megaman - Super.ips". Another way to check this
is if there are white squares on the title screen, the patch is not
applying.' s5.3 refuses a pack keyed for a patched ROM (#225) rather than
printing a figure, and on this game the refusal is not a formality:
UxROM with CHR RAM means the IPS patch's PRG changes travel through the
game's own loader into the tile data the pack was authored against
(ADR-0184 s1's hazard 1, measured there on Contra). A percentage of our
unpatched recordings against a patched game's art would be a number
nobody could act on, so this profile is scored by s5.1 alone and the
reference is reported as refused in RESULT.md.
No community MEP pack for this ROM is on disk either: the EnhancementPacks
folder holds only a .mep-install.json marker for 'Mega Man (USA)', with no
pack contents beside it.

navigation.label: the STAGE SELECT screen (SELECT STAGE / PRESS START) and its ring of six robot masters
navigation.source: The game's own STAGE SELECT screen, driven by input (ADR-0239 s1, first rung; ADR-0184 s3 rank 1, 'game code the developers shipped'). The Mega Man instruction booklet (Capcom USA, 1987; archive.org item 'mega-man-nes-manual') describes it: 'Six of MEGA MAN['s] ... enemies will be displayed on the TV/monitor screen. Player selects the character he chooses to challenge by pressing the control pad's tip ... Re-press START Button.' StrategyWiki's 'Mega Man/Walkthrough' names the buttons: 'You can switch between Robot Masters by pressing [Left/Right]. To select a stage, press [A/Start].' The ring order - CUTMAN, GUTSMAN, ICEMAN, BOMBMAN, FIREMAN, ELECMAN, then CUTMAN again - and the 240-frame settle the screen needs before it reads the pad are measured on this ROM on 2026-09-26, not published; see this file's _comment. No cheat: rung 1 needs none, and this profile pins nothing.

notes: Mega Man navigation sweep, ADR-0239: input selector (the STAGE SELECT screen and its ring of six robot masters), places swept Cut Man's stage, Guts Man's stage, Ice Man's stage, Bomb Man's stage, Fire Man's stage, Elec Man's stage. No cheat: the profile's own entry scripts select the place (ADR-0239 s1, first rung). Sources: the Mega Man instruction booklet (Capcom USA, 1987) for the screen and the two Starts, StrategyWiki 'Mega Man/Walkthrough' for the Left/Right and A/Start buttons, and this ROM's own screens on 2026-09-26 for the ring order and the settle.

The RAM checks read $0031, published as 'Stage ID' by Data Crystal's 'Mega Man (NES)/RAM map' ($00 = Cut Man ... $0B = Ending BG). Nothing is pinned, so no check carries ADR-0239 s4's pinned-byte caveat. The six expected values are measured on this ROM, not published; each session's own final state carries it.
_defaultsComment: The entry is mint-stage1.txt, which is both this profile's cutman value and
the game's own stage-1 route: power-on, Start to the select, then Start
again on the cursor the screen opens with - Cut Man. It is named for the
stage rather than the robot master because it is the route the stage set
declares (stage-set.json), and scripts/stages/README.md matches a route to
its mint by name prefix: `mint-stage1.txt` is what makes `stage1-run.txt`
recordable by the library job. It is defaults.entry rather than a value's
because it is the only entry that needs no cursor move at all; the other
The body is the game's one blind body: it runs right into whatever the
stage puts in the way, jumps, shoots, runs back left and does the same,
600 frames to a block. record_navigation_sweep.py repeats it until the
120 s budget is covered, which is ADR-0239 s6 and ADR-0184's amendment
both: effective input time, not a cheat, is what moves the picture. It
does not clear anything and is not meant to - the point of a navigation
session is which rooms and enemies the stage puts on screen.
